Plain Language Summary The India–Asia collision is among the most intriguing topics
Received 26 FEB 2021 in earth sciences because of its influence on global climate and Cenozoic topography. However, several
Accepted 9 JUN 2021 questions still remain unanswered, such as: how big was Greater India? When, where, and how did
the India collide with Asia? We report the first reliable early Eocene paleopole from the TH and assess
the timing of the India–Asia collision and the size of Greater India. Our results suggest a relatively
small Greater India, and that India collided with Asia at no later than 51–49.5 Ma. The constraints on
the India–Asia collision indicated by our data provide new boundary c∼onditions for the history of the
Himalayan–Tibetan orogen and global climate change.
1. Introduction
India–Asia collision and subsequent progressive convergence not only led to the closure of the Neo-Tethys
Ocean, but also produced the impressive and still active Himalayan–Tibetan orogen (Yin & Harrison, 2000).
Those geological events have had a long-term influence on Cenozoic topography, biogeography, and global
climate change (Kent & Muttoni, 2008; Raymo & Ruddiman, 1992; van Hinsbergen & Boschman, 2019). A
full understanding of when, where and how India collided with Asia is a key parameter in the evolution-
ary history of the Himalayan–Tibetan orogen and global climate change (Hu et al., 2016). However, there
are large uncertainties in the timing of the India–Asia collision; estimates range from as young as 34 Ma
(Aitchison et al., 2007) to as old as 70 Ma (Yin & Harrison, 2000), with most researchers preferring∼ a colli-
sional age of 50–55 Ma (Lippert e∼t al., 2014; Najman et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2015). The differences between
these estimat∼es arise not only from different collisional processes, but also from variable estimates of the
size of Greater India.
The traditional view is that India collided directly with Asia along the Indus–Tsangpo suture zone (ITSZ)
(Yin & Harrison, 2000), although Roy (1976) previously proposed that the Tethyan Himalaya (TH), a pos-
sible microcontinent, collided with Asia first, followed by collision of the Indian craton with the TH. This
© 2021. American Geophysical Union.
All Rights Reserved. dual-collision model has not been generally accepted by geologists because of the lack of supporting data.
BIAN ET AL. 1 of 24

### page_2
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2021JB021965
More recently, different collision models have been proposed. For example, van Hinsbergen et al. (2012)
integrated reliable paleomagnetic data from India, the Himalayas, and the Lhasa terrane (LT) and proposed
that the TH first collided with Asia at 50 Ma, after which the Indian craton collided with the TH at 25–
20 Ma with a closure of the Greater Ind∼ia Basin. Late Cretaceous and Paleocene paleomagnetic results ∼from
the TH led Yuan et al. (2021) to propose that the TH first collided with Asia at 61 Ma, and subsequently
the Indian craton collided with the TH at 53–48 Ma in a diachronous closure o∼f the North India Sea from
west to east. In addition, comprehensive g∼eological, geophysical and numerical modeling research prompt-
ed some researchers to propose different dual-collision models, in which the Indian craton collided with an
intraoceanic island arc prior to the terminal collision of the combined continent–arc with Asia (Aitchison
et al., 2007; Westerweel et al., 2019) or an intraoceanic arc collided with Asia at 50 Ma before the terminal
collision of the combined continent–arc with India at 45 Ma (Pusok & Steg∼man, 2020). Because these
dual-collision models are hard to reconcile with some g∼eological evidence, such as the existence of inde-
pendent terranes within the ITSZ and the discovery of a suture zone between the TH and Greater Himalaya,
these models have been the subject of heated discussion (Hu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2021).
Estimations of the size of Greater India, complementary methods, such as reconstructions of Mesozoic
Gondwana (Ali & Aitchison, 2005; Gibbons et al., 2012), the amount of crustal shortening within the Him-
alayas (DeCelles et al., 2002; Yi et al., 2011) and the northern extension of Greater India as a function of the
initial contact between India and Asia (Ma et al., 2017; van Hinsbergen et al., 2019; Yi et al., 2015), indicate
that the size of Greater India could have been anywhere between only a few hundred kilometers up to
3,400 km (Ali & Aitchison, 2005; DeCelles et al., 2002; van Hinsbergen et al., 2019; Meng et al., 2020). As
∼the India–Asia collision is approximately north-south along the ITSZ (Figure 1a), the key to solving these
problems is to reconstruct the precollisional paleogeography of the TH (the northern margin of India) and
the LT (the southern margin of Asia).
Paleomagnetism is the only tool for quantifying plate paleolatitudes, and is thus widely used to constrain
the kinematic processes of plate movement (Y. Chen et al., 1993; Liebke et al., 2010; Z. Li et al., 2016; Lippert
et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2019; Pozzi et al., 1982; Song et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2012). For the LT, the precollisional
paleogeography has been well constrained by a large number of Cretaceous to Eocene paleomagnetic data-
sets (Bian et al., 2020; Lippert et al., 2014; Yang, Ma, Zhang, et al., 2015a). For the TH, three reliable Early
Cretaceous paleomagnetic results obtained from lava flows (Bian et al., 2019; Yang, Ma, Bian, et al., 2015b;
Ma et al., 2016), which satisfied all the seven quality criteria of Van der Voo (1990), show an insignificant
paleolatitude difference between the TH and the Indian craton, indicating that the size of Greater India
was only a few hundred kilometers. However, four sets of reliable Late Cretaceous to Paleocene paleo-
magnetic results obtained from limestones in the TH indicate a large paleolatitude difference between the
TH and the Indian craton, suggesting that the size of Greater India was between 1,500 and 1,900 km
(Patzelt et al., 1996; Yi et al., 2011). The paleolatitudinal difference deduced from ∼the Late Cre∼taceous to
Paleocene paleomagnetic data is much larger than that inferred from the Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic
data, causing some researchers to suggest that a small ocean (basin) extended between the TH and the Indi-
an craton after the Early Cretaceous, and this oceanic basin extension further led to a dual-collision model
with an initial TH–Asia collision and a final Indian craton–TH collision (Ma et al., 2016; van Hinsbergen
et al., 2012; Yang, Ma, Bian, et al., 2015b). Because paleomagnetic data from the uppermost Cretaceous–
Paleogene limestones in the TH are critical to understanding the timing of India–Asia collision and the size
of Greater India, and widespread remagnetization has occurred in the carbonate rocks of the TH (Appel
et al., 2012; Tong et al., 2008), some researchers have reanalyzed the paleomagnetic data obtained from the
Zongshan Formation (Fm.) (71.0–65.0 Ma) and Zongpu Fm. (63.0–55.0 Ma) limestones (Huang, Lippert,
Zhang, et al., 2017; Yi et al., 2016). For example, the difference between the uniform reversed polarity of the
Characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) directions of the Zongshan Fm. limestone and the geomag-
netic polarity time scale (Ogg & Smith, 2004) during the time interval from the Turonian to Maastrichtian
prompted Yi et al. (2016) to suggest that the primary remanence of these rocks may have been completely
overprinted. Besides, thorough reanalysis of the reported ChRM directions of the Zongpu Fm. limestone,
together with rock magnetic and petrographic investigations led Huang, Lippert, Zhang, et al. (2017) to
propose that the limestone carries a synfolding or postfolding remanent magnetization.

More recently, Yang et al. (2019) obtained one Paleocene (60–58 Ma) paleomagnetic result from the Sang-
danlin redbeds in the northern TH, and suggested that the TH was located at 6.3° ± 4.3°S during 60–58 Ma.
In addition, Yuan et al. (2021) presented one Late Cretaceous (76.2–74.0 Ma) and one Paleocene (62.5–
59.2 Ma) paleomagnetic result in the TH, and suggested that the TH was located at 19.4°S at 75 Ma
and at 13.7°N at 61 Ma. Because the Indian craton moved northward at a very ra∼pid rate du∼ring the
Late Cr∼etaceous to ∼Paleogene (Copley et al., 2010; van Hinsbergen et al., 2011), conspicuous inconsisten-
cies existed for the Late Cretaceous to Paleogene paleomagnetic results of the TH (Huang, Lippert, Zhang,
et al., 2017; Patzelt et al., 1996; Yang et al., 2019; Yi et al., 2011, 2016; Yuan et al., 2021), and the lack of
reliable Eocene paleomagnetic results during the possible timing ( 50–55 Ma) of the India-Asia collision,
additional high-quality Late Cretaceous–Paleogene paleomagnetic d∼atasets with well-determined rock ages
are required to address these issues.
In this study, we report the first reliable early Eocene paleomagnetic study from the Zhepure Fm. limestone
in the TH (Figure 1b). Our new paleomagnetic results are a meaningful contribution to constraining the
precollisional paleogeography of the TH and estimating the size of Greater India, as well as clarifying the
timing of the India–Asia collision.
2. Geological Setting and Paleomagnetic Sampling
Our study region is located in the Duina–Gamba area of the TH where Paleogene marine strata are widely
exposed (Figure 1b). The Paleogene marine strata consist of, from oldest to youngest, the Jidula, Zongpu and
Zhepure Fms. Detailed descriptions of the Jidula and Zongpu Fms. were provided by Wan et al. (2002). The
Zhepure Fm. overlies the Zongpu Fm. with the boundary being a parallel unconformity. The Zhepure Fm.
can be divided into two parts. The lower part is mainly composed of gray microcrystalline limestone. The
upper part primarily consists of grayish-green and red silty shale intercalated with thin sandstone layers,
and muddy limestone. Our paleomagnetic sampling locations in the Duina and Gamba areas are the same
locations as described by Niu et al. (2016) in the Duina area and Wan et al. (2014) and Jiang et al. (2016) in
the Gamba area, respectively. The paleomagnetic samples were collected from the middle-upper Zhepure
Fm. limestone. These units were assigned to early Eocene age (Duina area) and Ypresian to Lutetian age
(Gamba area) based on paleontological data (Jiang et al., 2016; Niu et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2014). The detri-
tal zircon U–Pb chronological sample (DNS) in the Duina area was collected from a Zhepure Fm. sandstone
layer just located above the sampled Zhepure Fm. limestone (Figure 2a). The earliest folding of the studied
Eocene strata likely occurred at 45−24 Ma (Yin, 2006).
Samples were collected from 31 sites (DN1–DN31), from which a total of 319 cores were obtained near Dui-
na village (28°03′54.00″−28°03′59.57″N, 89°11′26.14″−89°11′52.30″E) in section A, located 65 km north-
east of Yadong County. Eleven sites (DB1–DB11), which yielded 117 cores, were drilled near ∼Gamba county
(28°16′57.34″N, 88°32′07.96″E) in section B, located 80 km northwest of section A. The bedding attitudes
of the Zhepure Fm. limestone are quite obvious at t∼hese two sections (Figure 2). The Zhepure Fm. lime-
stone in our studied area is mainly composed of nodular (Figures 2b, 2d, 2g and 2h), massive (Figure 2e),
and thin-bedded (Figure 2c) limestone. In general, every paleomagnetic site yielded 10 core samples and
spanned at least 70 cm of stratigraphic thickness.
All of the core samples were collected with a portable gasoline-powered drill, and oriented using a magnetic
compass and, weather permitting, a sun compass. The differences between the magnetic and sun compass
readings were usually within ±1°, revealing that magnetic disturbance in the sampling area can be ignored.
One fresh sandstone (sample DNS) was collected from a Zhepure Fm. sandstone layer for detrital zircon
U–Pb dating.
3. Methods
Oriented cores (2.5 cm diameter) were trimmed to standard 2.2-cm-high cylinders in the laboratory. Rema-
nent magnetizations were measured with a 2G-755-4K cryogenic magnetometer, and demagnetization was
performed using a Magnetic Measurements Thermal Demagnetizer Super Cooling (MMTDSC) furnace or
an ASC Scientific D-2000 alternating field (AF) demagnetizer. Approximately 97% of the specimens were
BIAN ET AL. 4 of 24

### page_5
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2021JB021965
Figure 2. Photographs showing field outcrops of the Zhepure Fm. limestone in the Duina (a–e) and Gamba (f–h)
areas. (b, d, g, and h) nodular limestone, (c) thin-bedded limestone, and (e) massive limestone.
BIAN ET AL. 5 of 24

### page_6
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2021JB021965
subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization, and 3% of specimens were treated with stepwise thermal
demagnetization up to 200°C followed by stepwise AF demagnetization up to 100 mT. In principle, thermal
demagnetization temperature intervals were set to 40°C below 280°C and changed to 30°C−10°C above
280°C; AF intervals were set to 2.5–5 mT before 30 mT and shifted to 10 mT steps after 30 mT. ChRM direc-
tions were calculated using principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) with at least four successive
steps. Site mean directions were determined using standard Fisherian statistics (Fisher, 1953). Published
computer program packages (Enkin, 1990; Cogné, 2003) were used to analyze the paleomagnetic data.
The acquisition and back-field demagnetization of isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM), as well as
three-axis IRM (Lowrie, 1990) were magnetized with an ASC IM10−30 pulse magnetizer and measured
using a JR-6A spinner magnetometer. The three-axis IRM was imparted successively at 2.4, 0.4, 0.12 T
along three orthogonal axes. The MMTDSC furnace, the D-2000 AF demagnetizer, and magnetometers are
housed in a magnetically shielded room with a residual magnetic field of less than 300 nT. These instru-
ments, as well as an ASC IM10−30 pulse magnetizer, are installed at the Paleomagnetism and Environmen-
tal Magnetism Laboratory of the China University of Geosciences, Beijing (CUGB). Hysteresis loops were
measured using a MicroMagTM Model 3,900 Vibrating Sample Magnetometer at the Paleomagnetism and
Geochronology Laboratory, Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (IGGCAS).
Polished thin sections were made from representative samples for microscopic observation. To further iden-
tify the microtextures and composition of the iron oxides, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations
and energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS) analyses were carried out with an acceleration voltage of 20 kV
and a working distance of 15.0 mm at the Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope Laboratory of the
CUGB, or with an acceleration voltage of 15 kV and a working distance of 8–9 mm at the Electron Micropro-
be Analysis and Scanning Electron Microscope Laboratory of the IGGCAS. To obtain high-quality images,
the polished samples were coated with platinum or carbon before analysis.
Detrital zircon U–Pb analyses were conducted by laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spec-
trometry (LA–ICP–MS) at Beijing Createch Testing Technology Co., Ltd, using an ESI NWR 193 nm laser
ablation system coupled with an Analytik Jena PQMS Elite ICP–MS instrument, following standard proce-
dures (Liu et al., 2010). A laser 25 μm in diameter with an energy density of 2.31 J/cm2 was used in these
analyses. Zircon GJ-1 was used as an external standard for U–Pb dating. U–Th–Pb concentrations were
calibrated using SRM 610 as an external standard and Si as an internal standard. Analyses with more than
15% discordance were excluded. We adopted 206Pb/238U and 207Pb/206Pb ages for grains younger and older
than 1,000 Ma, respectively.
4. Results
4.1. Zircon U–Pb Analytical Results
The zircons are rounded to subrounded (50–100 μm long, 30–50 μm wide) with clear oscillatory zoning in
most grains (Figure 3a). The Th/U ratios of the zircons (0.16–1.87) are higher than those of metamorphic
zircons (generally < 0.1) except for three zircon grains that had values of 0.06, 0.08, and 0.09 (Table S1).
These features indicate that magmatic rocks were the major sources of the zircon grains. Fifty-seven percent
of the analyses yielded Precambrian–Paleozoic ages, with 43% of grains exhibiting Mesozoic and Cenozoic
ages (Figure 3b). Younger zircons are clustered between 80 and 95 Ma, with the main peak between 85 and
90 Ma (n = 24 grains). Other younger zircons grouped between 65 and 70 Ma (n = 4 grains) or between
130 and 140 Ma (n = 5 grains; Table S1, Figure S1a). The youngest zircon age (52.6 ± 1.0 Ma) can be in-
terpreted as the maximum allowable depositional age of the Zhepure Fm., consistent with the conclusion
( 53–55 Ma) from detrital zircon U–Pb ages in the Gamba area (J. Li et al., 2015).
∼
4.2. Rock Magnetic Results
IRM acquisition curves of the Zhepure Fm. limestone showed a relatively rapid increase below 200 mT, and
saturation was not reached even at an applied field of 2.5 T (Figure 4). When reverse fields were applied,
the remanence decreased rapidly and reduced to zero between 40 and 170 mT (Figure 4), indicating that the
Zhepure Fm. limestone contains both low- and high-coercivity magnetic minerals. The Lowrie (1990) test

indicated that the high- and low-coercivity magnetic minerals unblocked at 680°C and 450°C were he-
matite and fine-grained magnetite (Cao et al., 2019; Dunlop & Özdemir, 2000∼), respectivel∼y (Figure 5). The
hysteresis loops are wasp-waisted in shape (Figure S2), which also supports the coexistence of the high- and
low-coercivity magnetic minerals in the Zhepure Fm. limestone.
4.3. Petrographic Results
The microscopic observations show that the Zhepure Fm. limestone contains abundant fossil foraminifera
(Figures 6a–6c). These foraminifera are well preserved, indicating that the studied limestone has not suf-
fered from significant deformation. SEM observations and EDS analyses indicated that the studied lime-
stone contains abundant Fe oxides (Figures 6d–6o). These Fe oxides usually occur as irregular shapes sev-
eral micrometers in size, with very clear boundaries with the surrounding carbonates. These observations,

4.4. Paleomagnetic Results
Representative Zijderveld (1967) diagrams of the Zhepure Fm. limestone are shown in Figure 7. Low tem-
perature components (LTC) or low coercivity components (LCC) can be isolated between 100°C and 300°C
or between 2.5 and 15 mT. Their mean direction in geographical coordinates (Figure S3) is clustered around
the present local geomagnetic field direction (D = 0.2°, I = 43.9°) and is considered to represent a viscous
remanent magnetization of the recent geomagnetic field. After removing the LTC or LCC, a stable high
temperature component (HTC) or a stable high coercivity component (HCC) decaying toward the origin
could be isolated using principal component analysis between 310°C and 450°C–580°C or between 20 mT
and 80–100 mT, and defines the ChRM. The ChRM directions include clear antipodal reversed (Figures 7a–
7h and 7l–7s) and normal (Figures 7i–7k) polarities. Noticeably, the normal (Figures 7i–7k) and reversed
(Figures 7a–7h, 7l–7p) polarities, which are both from section A, exhibit similar rock-magnetic properties
and demagnetization characteristics. Furthermore, a small number of specimens showed scattered demag-
netization patterns (Figure 7t); stable ChRM directions could not be isolated from them. Based on the fol-
lowing filtering criteria by excluding sites: (i) ChRM directions have α > 16°; (ii) site-mean direction
95
obtained from <5 specimens; (iii) the ChRM directions show an angular deviation of more than 45° from
the mean direction (sites DB9 and DB11), 30 out of 42 paleomagnetic sites provided the site-mean direction:
Dg = 333.4°, Ig = 31.4°, kg = 31.7, α = 4.7° in situ and Ds = 332.6°, Is = 20.1°, ks = 90.9, α = 2.8° after
95 95
tilt-correction, corresponding to a paleopole at 58.7°N, 330.3°E, A = 2.5° (Figure 8a, and Tables 1 and S2).
95
Application of fold tests (McElhinny, 1964; McFadden, 1990) indicated a positive result at 95% and 99%
confidence levels and yielded an optimal concentration at 106% unfolding (k = 91.5), which is commensu-
rate with the 100% unfolding (k = 90.9; Figure 8b). These results, combined with the positive reversal test
(McFadden & McElhinny, 1990), indicate that the ChRM directions preserve a primary origin.
To avoid the suspicion of a loose constraint of the positive fold and reversal tests because of the 80-km
distance between the two sections, we further tested whether section A passed the fold and rever∼sal tests
alone. The site-mean direction from section A (23 sites) is Dg = 339.0°, Ig = 35.1°, kg = 95.7, α = 3.1° in
95
situ and Ds = 335.2°, Is = 19.7°, ks = 289.1, α = 1.8° after tilt-correction, corresponding to a paleopole at
95
60.6°N, 326.5°E, A = 1.3° (Tables 1 and S2). This paleopole is very consistent with the paleopole (58.7°N,
95
330.3°E, A = 2.5°) obtained from 30 sites. Furthermore, this site-mean direction also passes the fold tests
95
of McElhinny (1964) and McFadden (1990) at 95% and 99% confidence levels, and yields an optimal con-
centration at 97.7% unfolding (k = 289.4), which is also commensurate with the 100% unfolding (k = 289.1;
Figure 8c). Furthermore, the site-mean direction passes the reversal test (McFadden & McElhinny, 1990),
with a B classification at the 95% confidence level. Both positive fold and reversal tests from section A fur-
ther increase our confidence in the reliability of the data.
4.5. Possible Inclination Shallowing
Although carbonate rocks are less prone to compaction (Huang, Lippert, Zhang, et al., 2017), a paleogeo-
graphic reconstruction made using paleomagnetic results from carbonate rocks should take the influence
of depositional and/or compaction-induced inclination shallowing into account (Dupont-Nivet et al., 2010;
Kodama, 2012; Ma et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2013). The Elongation/Inclination (E/I) method (Tauxe &
Kent, 2004) is widely used to identify and correct the degree of inclination deviation. Because only section
A from the Duina area includes more than 100 specimens, we performed E/I correction on the 160 inde-
pendent ChRM directions of section A. The sample-mean direction of section A is Ds = 335.3°, Is = 19.6°,
ks = 136.6, α = 1.0° (n = 160) after tilt-correction (Figure 9a). After applying the E/I correction, it shows
95
a flattening factor of 0.7 and yields a mean inclination of 27.6° (22.0°, 33.5°) (Figure 9a). This indicates that
the Zhepure Fm. limestone may have suffered from depositional and/or compaction-induced inclination
shallowing. Notably, unrecognized vertical-axis rotations within wide distribution of sampling sites may
led to an over-correction of inclination shallowing (Hillhouse, 2010; Kodama, 2012; Ma et al., 2018; Tong
et al., 2015), we excluded nine independent ChRM directions (red circles in Figure 9a) that showed more
than 16° angular deviations from the Fisher mean of the 160 sample-mean direction. The E/I correction of

the remaining 151 ChRM directions shows a flattening factor of 0.7, which is consistent with the flattening
factor obtained from 160 ChRM directions (Figure 9). The flattening factor of 0.7 is also in good agreement
with 0.69 ± 0.13 averaged for magnetite-bearing sediments and rocks (N = 13) (Kodama, 2012). Due to
identical directional behavior of the ChRM directions in sections A and B, the flattening factor of 0.7 was
used to correct all the inclinations obtained from the Zhepure Fm. limestone of the Duina-Gamba area.
After E/I correction, the site-mean direction is Ds = 332.7°, Is = 27.5°, ks = 81.8, α = 2.9°, corresponding
95
to a paleopole at 61.2°N, 337.3°E, A = 2.6°. This inclination-corrected paleopole was used for subsequent
95
paleogeographic interpretations.
5. Discussion
5.1. Age of the Sampling Zhepure Fm. Limestone
The Zhepure Fm. limestone does not contain volcanic rocks that would be suitable for precise dating. Fos-
sils identified in the limestone are of Ypresian–Lutetian age. However, because of the fast northward drift
of the TH during this period (Copley et al., 2010; van Hinsbergen et al., 2011), the paleontological dating
alone is not sufficient to satisfy the precise chronological limitations of paleomagnetism. Fortunately, mag-
netostratigraphy, together with paleontology and detrital zircon U–Pb geochronology, can be used to date
the strata.
The fossils (Alveolina; Figures 6a–6c) obtained at the base of the sampling Zhepure Fm. limestone (DN16)
in the Duina area have many species, and these species appeared from 56 Ma to 38.5 Ma in the Tethys
(Serra-Kiel et al., 1998). Furthermore, these fossils obtained from the D∼uina area a∼re the same as some of
microfacies 11 and 13 from the topmost Zongpu Fm. and the Zhepure Fm. limestone in the Gamba area as
described by J. Li et al. (2015). Biostratigraphic data from the Gamba area constrain the microfacies 11 and
13 to middle Ypresian (J. Li et al., 2015).
Our detrital zircon U–Pb analyses from the Duina area are broadly similar to those reported by J. Li
et al. (2015) from the Gamba area, and provide the youngest zircon age at 52.6 ± 1.0 Ma (Figures 3 and S1,
and Table S1). This youngest zircon age is also similar to the ages of 54.0 ± 1.0 Ma, 53.0 ± 1.0 Ma, and
55.0 ± 0.9 Ma reported by J. Li et al. (2015). J. Li et al. (2015) referred to these Eocene strata as the Enba
Fm. and Zhaguo Fm. from oldest to youngest, but these strata, which are coeval with the Zhepure Fm., were
named the Zhepure Fm. in the 1:250,000 scale Yadong–Jiangzi County regional geological survey report
(H45C004004 and G45C001004, 2005). To avoid confusion, we use the original nomenclature in this study.
Considering that (1) paleontological data and/or detrital zircon geochronology results from the Zhepure
Fm. strata date the boundary of the Zongpu and Zhepure Fms. at 56 Ma (Niu et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2014;
Wang et al., 2020) or at 51 Ma (J. Li et al., 2015); (2) our paleoma∼gnetic samples were drilled from the mid-
dle-upper Zhepure Fm. ∼limestone whose age should be much younger than 56 Ma; (3) all the paleomagnetic
samples from the upper part of the sampling Zhepure Fm. limestone show a reversed polarity and those
from its lower part (DN14–DN17) includes both reversed and normal polarities, we can reasonably corre-
late magnetozones R1−R2 and N1 to Chrons C23r.1r through C22r ( 51–49.5 Ma; Figure 8d) or to C24r.1r
through C23r.2r ( 53.2–52.0 Ma; Figure 8d). Noticeably, our magneto∼stratigraphic result shows that reverse
magnetozone R1 ∼is clearly longer than normal magnetozone N1 (Figure 8d). This is not consistent with
the fact that normal chron C24n.1n spans a duration which is almost equivalent to reversed chron C23r.2r.
Therefore, we prefer that the sampling Zhepure Fm. limestone was deposited at 51.0–49.5 Ma.

5.2. Late Cretaceous to Paleogene Paleolatitudes of the TH
Robust paleomagnetic datasets are a prerequisite for quantifying plate paleolatitudes. Available Late Creta-
ceous to Paleogene paleomagnetic datasets from the TH are summarized in Table 2, and the seven widely
applied quality criteria of Van der Voo (1990) were applied to assess the data. Accurate paleomagnetic
results require not only a sufficient number of samples (sites) to average paleosecular variation, but also
reliable field tests (such as a positive fold, conglomerate or contact test), the presence of reversals, or both,
to guarantee a primary magnetization. In this study, robust paleomagnetic data were identified by means of
at least one positive field test or the presence of reversals in addition to the other five quality criteria.
For the central-eastern TH, a total of nine available Late Cretaceous to Eocene paleopoles have been re-
ported (Table 2). A reference point (29.5°N, 91.0°E) located in the central-eastern part of the ITSZ was
used to calculate their paleolatitudes. Among them, three Late Cretaceous (CHD, CL, and ZS96), and four
Paleogene (ZP96, ZP1A, ZP1B, and DN) paleopoles satisfied our selection criteria. Notably, for the two Late
Cretaceous (CHD and ZS96) and three Paleocene (ZP96, ZP1A, and ZP1B) paleomagnetic results, because:
(1) the Chuangde Fm. limestone may have formed in a complex environment as a result of the studied
area experiencing 150° clockwise rotation relative to the Indian craton, as well as the possible inclination
shallowing has no∼t been identified and corrected for the limestone (Zhang et al., 2017); (2) rock magnetic
and petrographic results indicate that the limestones of the Zongshan and Zongpu Fms. may have suffered
from remagnetization (Yi et al., 2016; Huang, Lippert, Zhang, et al., 2017); although Yi et al. (2017) argued
that the remanence was most likely acquired shortly after deposition or during early diagenesis, they also
agreed that the comprehensive rock magnetic and petrographical analyses are robust evidence for a sec-
ondary origin of the magnetic carrier of the Zongpu Fm. limestone; Huang, Lippert, Jackson, et al. (2017)
further argued that the timing of remagnetization could not be demonstrated to early diagenetic stage, we
thus do not use these five paleopoles to constrain the paleolatitudes of the TH. Our new Eocene paleopole
(DN) of the Zhepure Fm. limestone, which is well constrained by magnetostratigraphy, paleontology and
detrital zircon U–Pb geochronology and satisfies all seven quality criteria, provides an inclination-corrected
site-mean paleopole at 61.2°N, 337.3°E with A = 2.6°, corresponding to a paleolatitude of 15.2 ± 2.6°N at
95
51–49.5 Ma for the reference point (29.5°N, 91.0°E). Furthermore, one Late Cretaceous paleopole (CL)
∼obtained from the Late Cretaceous (76.2–74.0 Ma) oceanic red beds in the Gyangze area (Yuan et al., 2021)
satisfies our selection criteria. Both the E/I correction (Tauxe & Kent, 2004) and the anisotropy-based in-
clination shallowing correction (Hodych & Buchan, 1994) yield a flattening factor of 0.7, and provides an
∼

For the western TH, a total of four available Late Cretaceous to Paleocene paleopoles have been published
(Table 2). A reference point at the longitude of 82.0°E and the same latitude of 29.5°N was used to calculate
their paleolatitudes. Among them, one Late Cretaceous (ZS20) and two Paleocene (SG and SDL) paleopoles
satisfied our selection criteria. The Late Cretaceous ( 71.0–69.0 Ma) paleopole (ZS20) of the Zongshan
Fm. limestone in the Zhada area (Meng et al., 2020) pr∼ovides a sample-mean paleopole at −33.4°N, 5.7°E
with dp/dm = 1.6°/3.2°, corresponding to a paleolatitude of 5.7 ± 1.6°N (Table 2) for the reference point
(29.5°N, 82.0°E). E/I correction (Tauxe & Kent, 2004) for the 73 HTC directions indicate that the Zongshan
Fm. limestone do not suffer from significant inclination shallowing. Notably, a large data set (n > 100) is
needed for the E/I correction to sufficiently represent the distribution of directions of the geomagnetic
field (Tauxe & Kent, 2004), we thus do not use this paleopole in further analysis. For the Paleocene (62.5–
59.2 Ma) paleopole (SG) of the red siliceous shales in the Saga area reported by Yuan et al. (2021), anisot-
ropy-based inclination shallowing correction (Hodych & Buchan, 1994) yields a flattening factor of 0.7,
provides a sample-mean paleopole at 74.0°N, 278.5°E with A = 2.5°, corresponding to a paleolatitu∼de of
95
14.1° ± 2.5°N (Table 2) for the reference point (29.5°N, 82.0°E). However, the Paleocene (60.0–58.0 Ma)
paleopole (SDL) in the Saga area reported by Yang et al. (2019) provides a site-mean paleopole at 55.9°N,
267.6°E with dp/dm = 2.8°/5.5°, corresponding to a paleolatitude of 4.5° ± 2.8°S (Table 2) for the reference
point (29.5°N, 91.0°E). After anisotropy-based inclination shallowing calibration (Hodych & Buchan, 1994),
the paleolatitude ranges from 4.5° ± 2.8°S to 7.3° ± 2.9°S. Yuan et al. (2021) showed that the sample-mean
direction of the middle temperature components (MTCs, Dg = 180.6°, Ig = −16.1° with α = 1.7° before
95
tilt correction, and Ds = 180.6°, Is = 16.9° with α = 1.7° after tilt correction) are similar to the HTCs
95

95 95
after tilt correction) obtained by Yang et al. (2019), and argued that the HTCs of Yang et al. (2019) can-
not be used for paleogeographic reconstructions. Notably, there are some differences existed between Yang
et al. (2019) and Yuan et al. (2021). For example, (1) the sampling units of Yang et al. (2019) came from

both Sangdanlin and Zheya Fms., whereas the sampling units of Yuan et al. (2021) came from Sangdanlin
Fm.; (2) the sampling units of Yang et al. (2019) were assigned to 60–58 Ma based on zircon U-Pb ages and
biostratigraphy (DeCelles et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2015), and the sam∼pling units of Yuan et al. (2021) were as-
signed to 62.5–59.2 Ma based on magnetostratigraphy combined with biostratigraphy and zircon U-Pb ages
(DeCelles et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2014); (3) the HTCs were isolated between 500°C–600°C and
640°C–680°C and they were decayed toward the origin (Figure 6 in Yang et al., 2019), whereas the MTCs
were isolated between 300°C–650°C and they were not decayed toward the origin (Figures 3d–3f in Yuan
et al., 2021); (4) the HTCs obtained by Yang et al. (2019) yielded a paleolatitude of 7.3° ± 2.9°S, whereas
the HTCs obtained by Yuan et al. (2021) yielded a paleolatitude of 14.1 ± 2.5°N; (5) the complex geological
structure such as faults are observed in the field outcrop (Figure 2a in Yang et al. (2019)). Thus, it is difficult
to estimate the differences existed between Yang et al. (2019) and Yuan et al. (2021), and we consider that
further paleomagnetic investigations with well-determined rock ages are still required to resolve the issues
mentioned above. Considering that the India-Asia collision may have been diachronous (Liang et al., 2012;
Rowley, 1996; Wu et al., 2014), and our data comes from the central-eastern TH, we only consider the cen-
tral-eastern collision in this study.
5.3. The Size of Greater India
The timing of the India–Asia collision is one of the most significant boundary conditions in understand-
ing the evolutionary history of the Himalayan–Tibetan orogen (Aitchison et al., 2007). To determine the
time of collision between India and Asia, it is first necessary to know the size of Greater India. One way
to assess the size of Greater India is to determine the amount of crustal shortening within the Himalaya,
which can be estimated by comparing the paleolatitudes observed from the TH with coeval paleolatitudes
expected from the Indian craton for the same reference point (Patzelt et al., 1996; Yi et al., 2011). Our new
Eocene paleopole (DN) of the Zhepure Fm. limestone satisfies all seven quality criteria, and provides an in-
clination-corrected paleolatitude of 15.2° ± 2.6°N for the reference point (29.5°N, 91.0°E) at 51–49.5 Ma.
Comparing this result with the coeval paleolatitude (4.8° ± 2.8°N, 50 Ma, Table 2) for the I∼ndian craton
(Torsvik et al., 2012) gives a paleolatitudinal difference of 10.4° ± 3.8° (Figure 10a), indicating that north-
south crustal shortening of 1,140 ± 420 km has occurred w∼ithin the central-eastern Himalayas since 50 Ma.
Our results suggest a relatively small Greater India during the early Eocene. Similarly, the Late Cretaceous
paleopole (CL) provides an inclination-corrected paleolatitude of −18.4° ± 1.8°N for the reference point
(29.5°N, 91.0°E) at 75 Ma (Yuan et al., 2021). The Indian craton was located at −30.3° ± 2.9°N at 80 Ma
and at −23.5° ± 2.5°∼N at 70 Ma for the reference point (29.5°N, 91.0°E). Interpolating an average velocity of
7.5 cm/yr between 80 and 70 Ma, the Indian craton was located at −26.6° ± 2.5°N at 75 Ma. Comparing
∼this paleolatitude with the coeval paleolatitude (−18.4° ± 1.8°N, 75 Ma, Table 2) observed from the TH
gives a paleolatitudinal difference of 8.2° ± 3.1° (Figure 10a), ind∼icating that north-south crustal shorten-
ing of 900 ± 340 km has occurred wi∼thin the central-eastern Himalayas since 75 Ma. The 900 ± 340 km
calculated from the Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic results agrees well with the 1∼,140 ± 420 km north-south
crustal shorting inferred from our new paleomagnetic results.
The 900–1,140 km north-south crustal shortening documented by the Eocene and Late Cretaceous paleo-
magn∼etic results is basically consistent with the amount of crustal shortening inferred from other geological
evidence; for example, balanced cross-section analyses show that the Himalayas underwent crustal shorten-
ing of 400–700 km (DeCelles et al., 2002; Yin & Harrison, 2000). In addition, based on the reconstruction
of east∼ern Gondwana and bathymetric results from the southeastern Indian Ocean, the size of the central
part of Greater India was 950 km, and the eastern and western parts were no more than 500 and 600 km
in size, respectively (Ali &∼ Aitchison, 2005). Analysis of seafloor anomalies, fracture zones, and crustal ages
from the west Australian margin and the Wharton Basin indicate that the major extension of Greater India
was located at the Wallaby–Zenith Fracture Zone, requiring a Greater Indian extent of 1,200 km (Gibbons
et al., 2012). ∼
5.4. The Timing of India-Asia Collision
The paleolatitudinal overlap of the LT with the TH is one of the most direct ways to assess the timing of the
collision. For the LT, Bian et al. (2020) summarized all the reliable Cretaceous paleomagnetic datasets of

Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2021JB021965
Figure 10. Paleolatitudinal evolution of the Indian craton, the TH, and the LT. (a) The shaded areas and vertical bars show the errors of the paleolatitudes.
The expected and observed paleolatitudes were calculated for the reference point at (29.5°N, 91.0°E). (b–c) Paleogeographic reconstructions of the India–Asia
collision at 75 and 50 Ma based on the relative plate reconstruction of Matthews et al. (2016). LT, Lhasa terrane; TH, Tethyan Himalaya; GI, Greater India.
∼ ∼
the LT, and applied three methods (small circle fitting, inclination-only means and syntectonic-sedimenta-
tion-correction) to calculate the Cretaceous paleolatitude of the LT, and suggested that the southern mar-
gin of Asia had an east-west alignment in present-day coordinates before India-Asia collision. Considering
that (1) the LT remained at a relatively stable paleolatitude since the Early Cretaceous (Yang, Ma, Zhang,
et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2021); (2) the India-Asia collision may have been diachronous (Liang et al., 2012;
Rowley, 1996; Wu et al., 2014); (3) the Cretaceous paleolatitude of the central-eastern and western LT
obtained by three methods is indistinguishable with each other (Bian et al., 2020); (4) the paleolatitudes
obtained by small circle fitting method of the central-eastern LT (13.7° ± 3.6°N) cover that of the west-
ern LT (14.6° ± 2.3°N), the paleolatitude obtained by small circle fitting method of the central-eastern LT
(13.7° ± 3.6°N) was used as the southern margin of Asia before the India–Asia collision (Figures 10 and S4,
Table 2).
BIAN ET AL. 20 of 24

### page_21
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2021JB021965
The Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic results show that the TH was located at −18.4° ± 1.8°N for the reference
point (29.5°N, 91.0°E) at 75 Ma (Yuan et al., 2021). Comparing this latitude with 13.7° ± 3.6°N calculated
from the central-eastern ∼LT reveals a latitudinal difference of 32.1° ± 4.0° for the reference point (29.5°N,
91.0°E), demonstrating that the width of Neo-Tethys ocean was 3,530 ± 440 km (Figures 10a and 10b). Our
new paleomagnetic results indicate that the TH was located at 15.2° ± 2.6°N at 51–49.5 Ma for the ref-
erence point (29.5°N, 91.0°E). Comparison of our new paleomagnetic results with∼ paleolatitudes observed
from the central-eastern LT (13.7° ± 3.6°N) indicates that no significant paleolatitudinal difference existed
at 51–49.5 Ma. This demonstrates that the timing of the India–Asia collision occurred at no later than
5∼1–49.5 Ma (Figures 10a and 10c).
∼
This collisional age is consistent with the paleomagnetic results estimated by Lippert et al. (2014) and is com-
patible with other geological information, such as: (1) the enhanced sediment accumulation rate ( 20 cm/
kyr) at 52–48 Ma in the Gonjo Basin, east-central Tibet (S. Li et al., 2020); (2) the significant veloc∼ity drop
of India at 52–45 Ma (Cande & Stegman, 2011); (3) the cessation of marine sedimentation and the first
arrival of As∼ian material in the TH at 50 Ma (Najman et al., 2010); (4) a high CO concentration and warm
2
climate conditions at 50 Ma may be ∼attributed to the collision of India with Asia (Kent & Muttoni, 2008).
∼
6. Conclusions
We present the first reliable early Eocene paleomagnetic results from the Zhepure Fm. limestone in the
central-eastern TH, which provide important insights into the India–Asia collision and the size of Greater
India. The new paleomagnetic data pass both fold and reversal tests, indicating that the ChRM directions
are primary magnetizations acquired before folding. The tilt-corrected site-mean direction is Ds = 332.6°,
Is = 20.1°, ks = 90.9, α = 2.8° (N = 30). The site-mean inclination increased from 20.1° to 27.5° after in-
95
clination shallowing correction, giving a paleopole at 61.2°N, 337.3°E, A = 2.6° and a corresponding pale-
95
olatitude of 15.2° ± 2.6°N for the reference point (29.5°N, 91.0°E). The magnetostratigraphy, paleontology,
and detrital zircon U–Pb geochronology constrain the age of the studied strata to 51–49.5 Ma. The results
of the present study, together with reliable Cretaceous to Paleogene paleomagneti∼c results from the TH, LT,
and Indian craton, allow us to draw the following conclusions: (1) there was 900–1,140 km of north-south
crustal shortening existed between the Indian craton and TH; and (2) India∼ collided with Asia at no later
than 51–49.5 Ma.
∼
